title: File organisation and access
overview: File organisation describes how records are arranged on backing storage; file access describes how they are reached. You must compare serial, sequential and random organisation, understand direct access and indexing, and use hashing—including what happens when collisions occur.
syllabusPoints: Compare serial, sequential and random file organisation.
Select sequential or direct access for a stated use.
Explain indexes and how they can reduce search time.
Use a hashing algorithm to calculate record addresses and explain collision handling.

definitions.definition: Records are stored in the order they arrive, with no ordering by key.
Records are stored in order of a key field.
Records are stored at locations calculated or chosen to allow direct access.
A smaller structure mapping search keys to record locations.
An algorithm that transforms a record key into a storage address.
Two different keys generate the same hash address.

sections.title: Serial organisation
content: Very simple for append-heavy data such as logs. New records can be added quickly, but finding one record usually means reading from the start until it is found.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.content: Example: a transaction log written in time order.

sections.title: Sequential organisation
content: Records are kept sorted by a key. This is effective for batch processing in key order and allows ordered traversal. Insertion/update can be more expensive because ordering must be preserved.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.content: Example: employee records stored in EmployeeID order for payroll processing.

sections.title: Random organisation and direct access
content: The program can jump directly to a likely record location rather than reading every previous record. It suits systems that repeatedly retrieve individual records by a unique key.

sections.title: Indexes
content: An index stores keys plus pointers/addresses. Searching the smaller index identifies where the full record is stored. Extra storage and maintenance are required, especially when records are inserted or deleted.

sections.title: Hashing
content: A hash function transforms a key into an address. A good function is fast and spreads keys across the available range. The same function must be used on retrieval.

sections.title: Collision resolution
content: Because the address range is finite, collisions are unavoidable. The system needs a defined rule such as linear probing, an overflow area or chaining. Retrieval must follow the same collision rule used during insertion.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.content: If slot 231 is occupied, linear probing can test 232, 233, ... until a free slot is found.

formulas.label: Simple hash address
formulas.note: A complete answer must also explain how collisions are handled.

examTips: Name both the organisation/access method and the scenario-specific reason.
Show the hash calculation and then explain collision handling.
Random access does not mean 'stored randomly'; addresses are determined systematically.
commonMistakes: Confusing file organisation with file access.
Ignoring collisions after calculating the hash address.
Using a different hash/collision rule for retrieval than insertion.
